findings.explanation: Each manager owns an array and appends one record per use call. With no options object, synchronous defaults to false and runWhen to null; when an options object exists, its field values are stored verbatim, including undefined. The returned ID is the record's zero-based array index. eject replaces an existing record with null without shrinking the array, so later registrations append after the hole and receive increasing IDs. Iteration proceeds in array order and skips null slots. clear replaces the array with an empty one, discarding all slots and causing subsequent IDs to restart at zero, so old numeric IDs can be reused.

During each request's chain assembly, every non-ejected request interceptor whose runWhen is a function is called with the current assembled config. It is skipped only when the result is strictly false; other results remain eligible. Skipping happens before synchronous-mode calculation, so skipped interceptors cannot force Promise mode. The mode flag starts true and is ANDed with every eligible request interceptor's synchronous value: all eligible request interceptors must be truthy-synchronous, while an empty eligible set remains synchronous. Managers iterate in registration order, but unshift makes request pairs execute newest-first. Response pairs are pushed and therefore execute oldest-first. Response records are neither runWhen-filtered nor consulted for synchronous-mode selection, so their stored options do not affect that decision.

If any eligible request interceptor is not synchronous, Axios starts with Promise.resolve(config) and attaches pairs in this order: newest-to-oldest request interceptors, dispatch, then oldest-to-newest response interceptors. Standard Promise chaining governs every stage: a returned value fulfills the next stage, a returned promise or thenable is adopted, and a throw or rejected return rejects the next stage. A rejection callback can recover by returning a value; if it is missing, throws, or returns a rejection, the error continues. Because fulfilled and rejected callbacks are arguments to the same then call, the rejected callback does not catch a throw from its own paired fulfilled callback; that throw is observable only by a later stage's rejection callback.

In synchronous mode, fulfilled handlers are ordinary direct calls, newest-first, and each successful return immediately replaces newConfig. If one throws, its own paired rejection callback is invoked immediately with the Axios instance as its receiver—unlike the Promise path. That callback's return value is ignored and is not awaited; if it returns normally, Axios stops running the remaining request interceptors and proceeds to dispatch with the last successfully assigned config. Earlier replacements and any in-place mutations made before the throw survive. If the rejection callback is missing, accessing call throws a TypeError; if it throws, that new error escapes. In either case _request exits before dispatch and before response handlers are attached, and the async public request boundary converts/rethrows it as a rejected public request promise.

After dispatch normally returns a promise, response pairs are attached in registration order. Fulfilled results and adopted promises flow forward; a rejection callback may recover by returning a value, while a throw or rejected return continues to a later rejection callback. The final recovered value resolves the public request; an unrecovered error is awaited and rethrown by the public request boundary. In synchronous-request mode, an asynchronously rejected dispatch promise is returned normally first, so response rejection handlers are attached and may recover it. A synchronous dispatch throw instead enters this catch and returns Promise.reject before the response-attachment loop, so no response interceptor can observe it. In Promise-request mode, dispatch itself is an earlier then stage and response stages are already in the assembled chain: both a synchronously thrown dispatch error and a returned asynchronously rejected promise become downstream rejections that response handlers can process.
